kurz: How valuation and profitability ratios are formed as a fraction of numerator and denominator, and what information is lost in the process.

bloecke.md:
A financial ratio condenses a two-hundred-page annual report into a single number. Everything that does not go into the formula is lost in the process. Even so, ratios are very useful. They make companies of different sizes comparable, they show developments over time, and they let you narrow a market of thousands of securities down to a handful of candidates.

Ratios do not, however, answer the question of why a number looks the way it does. They fall into two groups that must not be mixed. **Valuation ratios** relate a price to an earnings measure and show how expensive a company is. **Profitability ratios** relate a result to the capital employed and show how good the business is. A company can be excellent and too expensive at the same time. Investors who mix the two groups easily mistake high quality for a low price.

## The numerator-denominator rule

All valuation ratios follow a common construction rule. Numerator and denominator must belong to the same group of claimholders. The share price and market capitalisation belong to the owners, so they are paired with **equity measures** such as net profit, book value and earnings per share. The [[Enterprise value|enterprise value]] belongs to all providers of capital together, so it is paired with **total capital measures** such as revenue, EBIT and [[EBITDA]].

The enterprise value is the price of the operating business, regardless of who financed it. It equals market capitalisation plus [[Net financial debt|net financial debt]]. Anyone buying a heavily indebted company takes over its debt as well, and anyone buying a company with a very large cash position also receives that cash. This is why the same share can be cheap on its P/E ratio and expensive on EV/EBIT.

bloecke.titel: From market capitalisation to enterprise value
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for the engineering company from the previous lessons. If pension provisions are included, the price of the operating business rises by just under 9%.

bloecke.md: Share price and market capitalisation go with equity measures (profit, book value, earnings per share), and enterprise value goes with total capital measures (revenue, EBIT, EBITDA). An “EV/net profit” or a “price/EBITDA” is therefore wrongly defined and not a conservative or aggressive variant of a correct ratio.

All ratios here are worked through for a single case, the model engineering company from the two previous lessons. Its key figures are: revenue €1,000 million, EBITDA 235, EBIT 160, interest expense 25, tax rate 30%, net profit 94.5, balance sheet total 1,100, equity 385, financial liabilities 310, cash and securities 80. The subscribed capital of €60 million corresponds to 60 million shares, as each no-par-value share represents one euro of it. The share price is €25.20.

This gives earnings per share of €1.575, a book value per share of €6.42 and a market capitalisation of €1,512 million. All other ratios are obtained by division.

bloecke.md: Net financial debt is not a standardised measure. You can, for example, add the pension provisions of 150 million. This is justifiable because they are interest-bearing obligations. The enterprise value then rises to 1,892 and EV/EBIT from 10.9 to 11.8. Since IFRS 16, lease liabilities have also been included in financial debt, and lease expenses no longer reduce EBITDA. Two data providers can therefore report EV/EBITDA figures for the same company on the same day that differ by 20%. Before any peer comparison, you should check the definition and not adopt the figure unchecked.

## Limits of price multiples

The **P/E ratio** depends heavily on its denominator. Net profit includes one-off items, fair value changes, tax effects and the consequences of financing. A one-off property sale lowers the P/E ratio without the business having improved. With cyclical companies, the signal is even reversed. A steel group with a P/E ratio of 5 is usually at its earnings peak, one with a P/E ratio of 30 at the low point of the cycle.

The **P/B ratio** compares the price with the equity shown on the balance sheet. It is useful where the balance sheet reflects the business well, for example at banks, insurers and property companies. It says little where the value comes from research, brands and software. Most of this spending is booked as an expense, and that part does not appear as an asset. Research costs and internally generated brands may never be capitalised, development costs only under certain conditions (IAS 38, Sections 248(2), 255(2a) HGB (Commercial Code)). A P/B ratio of 9 for a software company is therefore not a sign of a bubble. The high value is a result of the accounting.

The **P/S ratio** is a stopgap for companies without profits. It assumes a margin that does not yet exist. It also breaks the numerator-denominator rule, because revenue is a total capital measure. The correct form is EV/revenue, in the model 1,742 / 1,000 = 1.74. The **PEG** is the P/E ratio divided by expected earnings growth as a percentage. It looks convincing but depends entirely on an estimate. If you assume 7% growth instead of 10%, the PEG rises from 1.6 to 2.3. It also takes neither risk nor return on capital into account. Growth bought with a lot of capital counts just as much as growth that costs nothing.

## Profitability ratios and their denominators

Profitability ratios differ only in whose capital is in the denominator. **ROE** measures the return on equity and is the owners' ratio. In the German definition, **ROA** adds back interest on debt and so measures the return on all capital employed, regardless of how it is financed. **ROCE** relates EBIT to long-term capital employed, that is, the balance sheet total minus current liabilities. In the model, that is 1,100 minus 260, or 840. **ROIC** relates after-tax operating profit to invested capital. This profit is called NOPAT and is calculated as EBIT times (1 − tax rate). Excess liquidity does not count as invested capital, because the interest income from it is not included in EBIT.

ROE is the most popular of these four ratios and at the same time the most vulnerable. It can be raised without any operational improvement. A debt-financed share buyback shrinks the equity in the denominator and so increases the ratio. The DuPont decomposition, developed at the company DuPont in 1919, makes such effects visible.

bloecke.formel: ROE = (Net profit / Revenue) × (Revenue / Balance sheet total) × (Balance sheet total / Equity)
bloecke.erklaerung: ROE equals net margin times asset turnover times equity multiplier. The first two factors describe the business, the third only the balance sheet structure.
variablen: how much of revenue is left over as profit
how many times a year the assets employed turn over into revenue
balance sheet total divided by equity, that is, the leverage

bloecke.titel: ROE broken down into business and financial leverage
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with orders of magnitude typical of each sector. The lower part of each bar shows margin times turnover, the upper part only the effect of financial leverage.

bloecke.md: The regional bank achieves almost 10% ROE, although arithmetically only one percentage point of it comes from its business. Nine tenths of its return on equity come from balance sheet leverage. For banks, this is part of the business model and not a flaw. It does explain, however, why the ROE of a bank and the ROE of a software company do not contain the same information. Leverage amplifies falls in earnings just as strongly as increases.

bloecke.formel: ROE = ROA + (ROA − Interest rate on debt) × Debt / Equity
bloecke.erklaerung: As long as the return on total capital is above the interest rate on debt, every additional unit of debt increases ROE. If it falls below that rate, the same leverage lowers ROE just as strongly.
bloecke.beispiel: ROA 10%, interest rate on debt 4%, debt/equity = 2.33: ROE = 10 + (10 − 4) × 2.33 = 24%

bloecke.md:
Both companies have total capital of 1,000 million and generate EBIT of 100 million. Company A is debt-free. Company B has 700 million of debt at 4% and only 300 million of equity.

- In a good year (EBIT 100), A earns 100 on equity of 1,000, or 10%. B pays 28 in interest and keeps 72 on equity of 300, which is 24%. On ROE, B looks 2.4 times as good as A.
- In a bad year (EBIT 30), A achieves 3%. B still pays 28 in interest and keeps 2, which is 0.7%.

The operating business was identical in both cases. B's higher ROE in the good year is based solely on a balance sheet decision and says nothing about the quality of the business.

Of the four return ratios, ROIC is therefore the most meaningful when it comes to the quality of a business, because financing decisions barely affect it. A company that earns 18% on its invested capital over ten years almost inevitably has an advantage that competitors have been unable to copy. Whether this creates value, however, only becomes clear from the comparison with the cost of capital. That calculation follows in the valuation module.

In practice, errors are particularly common in ratios that combine a flow for the year (revenue, profit) with a stock at the reporting date (equity, balance sheet total, inventories). Such ratios should be calculated using **average balances** from the beginning and end of the year. Otherwise, a capital increase in December leads to an artificially low ROE, and an acquisition in November to an artificially low asset turnover.

## Cash flow and payout ratios

The **FCF yield** is free cash flow divided by market capitalisation. It is the most direct yield indicator there is, because it depends least on accounting discretion. Its only weak point is its dependence on a single year. A company that postpones investment or reduces inventories generates a very high free cash flow as a one-off. A three-year average or the owner earnings calculation is more robust than the figure for a single reporting year.

The **payout ratio** relates the dividend to profit and is 40% in the model case. More meaningful is the cash payout ratio, which compares the dividend with free cash flow. Here that is 37.8 of 90 million, or 42%. Ratios above 100% are financed from existing assets or from debt and are rarely sustainable over time. The **dividend yield** of 2.5% is a pre-tax figure. After flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) of 25% plus solidarity surcharge (Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act), Section 43 EStG), 26.375% in total, 1.84% remains, provided the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 (Section 20(9) EStG) has already been used up. At company level, the profit had already been taxed with corporation tax (Section 23(1) KStG (Corporation Tax Act)), solidarity surcharge and trade tax (Gewerbesteuer; Section 11(2) GewStG (Trade Tax Act)), at 30% in the model.

bloecke.titel: Price-to-book ratio versus return on equity, US industries
bloecke.unter: Damodaran industry data, as of January 2026. An industry's P/B ratio depends almost entirely on its return on equity.

bloecke.md: For financial companies, this relationship can be written approximately as a formula: P/B = (ROE − g) / (cost of equity − g). A P/B ratio above 1 is only justified for a bank if its ROE is above its cost of equity. A P/B ratio of 0.7 for a bank with 6% ROE and a 10% cost of equity is therefore no bargain. According to the formula, this value is, if anything, already generous.

bloecke.unter: Damodaran, as of January 2026. There is a factor of four between oil production and semiconductors, so a comparison across these industry boundaries tells you nothing.

bloecke.md: Damodaran aggregates all companies listed in the US and also includes loss-making companies. He divides the sum of all market values by the sum of all earnings. The trailing P/E of the S&P 500, by contrast, stood at 26.64 on 13 October 2026 (multpl.com). It is based on a different basket and a different method. Aggregate market multiples, index multiples and industry medians can differ by a factor of two. Mixing multiples from different sources is one of the most common unnoticed errors in comparison tables.

- For a cyclical company at its earnings peak, the P/E ratio is lowest precisely when the profit cannot be repeated. The remedy is normalised earnings over a full cycle.
- For a structurally shrinking business, a P/E ratio of 7 is appropriate if profit falls by 10% every year. Whether a share is cheap can only be judged in relation to future earnings.
- A high dividend yield usually results from a fallen share price and not from a raised dividend. Before treating it as income, you should check the payout ratio against free cash flow.
- A low P/B ratio says little without a look at ROE. Book value does not set a price. Without a return above the cost of capital, it has hardly any significance for valuation.

Negative denominators produce meaningless values. A P/E ratio for a loss-making company is undefined and not simply a large number. Some data providers then show no value at all, others a negative value that is treated as a very cheap value when sorting. The same applies to negative equity (P/B ratio and ROE are then unusable, even though negative equity also occurs at companies with solid cash flows that buy back a lot of shares) and to a PEG with negative expected growth. Before any screening, you should therefore check how the provider handles negative denominators. Otherwise you filter out the cases you wanted to find and keep the ones you wanted to avoid.

A single ratio is not enough to reach a judgement. Its value lies in making deviations visible, for example compared with the company's own history, with its industry or with what the business model would lead you to expect. Where a figure deviates markedly, that is where the closer analysis begins.

mitnehmen: Numerator and denominator must belong to the same group of claimholders, so the share price goes with equity measures and the enterprise value with total capital measures.
A high ROE only says something about quality once the three-factor DuPont decomposition has established how much of it comes from financial leverage.
ROIC is the financing-neutral return ratio and therefore the best single indicator of the quality of a business model.
Comparisons across sector boundaries are not meaningful, because in the US data EV/EBIT ranges from around 10 for oil producers to over 44 for semiconductors.
For every ratio that looks cheap, check whether the earnings figure in it is repeatable, because at the earnings peak of a cycle the share with the lowest P/E ratio is the most expensive.

begriffe.text: Price of the entire operating business, calculated as market capitalisation plus net financial debt. It is set in relation to total capital measures such as EBIT, EBITDA and revenue, never to net profit.
Breakdown of ROE into net margin, asset turnover and equity multiplier. It shows whether a return on equity comes from pricing power, from efficiency or only from debt.

Return on invested capital, that is, NOPAT (EBIT after tax) divided by invested capital excluding excess liquidity. It is largely independent of the financing structure and therefore the most reliable single indicator of business quality.
Free cash flow divided by market capitalisation. It is the most direct yield indicator, but vulnerable to individual years with postponed investment or a reduction in working capital.

A share that looks cheap on the basis of ratios because the earnings figure in the ratio cannot be repeated. Examples are the profit of a cyclical company at the peak or the dividend of a shrinking business.
